title: Reading the script
summary: How vowel signs attach to letters, when the built-in a is silent, how letters join, and what the dot on top does.

sections.heading: Vowel signs (matras)
sections.body:
Every consonant carries a built-in short **a**: ક is ka. To give it a different vowel, you add a small sign called a matra. The sign replaces the built-in a.

One sign is written **before** the letter but said after it: કિ is ki, not ik.

sections.heading: When the built-in a goes silent
sections.body:
At the end of a word the built-in a is usually not said: ઘર is ghar, not ghara. Inside longer words it often drops too: છોકરો is chhokro, and વાંચવું is vaanchvun.

After a joined letter at the end of a word, the a is kept: મિત્ર is mitra. The transliteration in this app always shows what people actually say, so trust it over a letter-by-letter reading.

sections.heading: Joined letters
sections.body:
When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, the first one loses its a and the two are written as one joined shape, usually with half of the first letter: સ and ત make સ્ત in નમસ્તે. When letters can't join neatly, a small stroke under the first one (ક્) shows that it has no vowel.

A few joins have their own shapes, so learn them as new letters: ક્ષ (ksh), જ્ઞ (gn), ત્ર (tr), શ્ર (shr).

sections.heading: The dot on top (anusvara)
sections.body: A dot above a letter, as in હું, is called the anusvara. It makes the vowel nasal, a little like the French word bon. Before another consonant it often sounds like n or m: મંદિર is mandir. This app always writes it as **n**.

title: Am, is, are
summary: The words for I, you, he, she, we and they, and the form of "to be" that goes with each.

sections.heading: I am, you are
sections.body:
The verb goes at the end of a Gujarati sentence: "I home-at am". The word for am / is / are changes with the person.

In everyday speech તે is often said **એ**, and તેઓ is often **એ લોકો** (those people).
table: you are (polite, or more than one)

sections.heading: Two words for we
sections.body: **અમે** means "we, but not you": me and my family, say, without the person I'm talking to. **આપણે** means "we, including you". English has one word, so learners often mix them up, and getting it right sounds very natural.

sections.heading: Three ways to say you
sections.body:
**તું** is for people very close to you: friends, younger brothers and sisters, children, and God in prayer. **તમે** is the safe choice for elders, strangers and anyone you respect, and it is also the plural "you". **આપ** is extra respectful, for speeches, signs and formal moments; it takes છો, like તમે.

Calling an elder તું sounds rude, so when you're not sure, use તમે.

title: Nouns: gender and plurals
summary: Every Gujarati noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the ending often tells you which.

sections.heading: Three genders
sections.body:
Gujarati has three genders: masculine, feminine and neuter (neither). Every noun has one, not just people: રોટલી (flatbread) is feminine and ઘર (house) is neuter. Many nouns show their gender in their last sound.

Nouns that end in a consonant or in -aa don't give it away: ઘર is neuter, દિવસ (day) is masculine, ચા (tea) is feminine. A few break the pattern, like પાણી (water), which ends in -ee but is neuter. Learn each noun with મારો, મારી or મારું in front of it.

sections.heading: Making plurals
sections.body:
Each gender makes its plural its own way. Masculine -o becomes -aa, neuter -un becomes -aan, and feminine nouns add ઓ.

Masculine and neuter nouns that end in a consonant usually stay the same, and a number or the verb shows there's more than one. You can also add ઓ to almost any plural to make it extra clear: છોકરાઓ (boys), ઘરો (houses).

examples.en: There are four crows on the tree.
There are two girls in the house.

title: Describing words
summary: Adjectives like સારું (good), whose dictionary form ends in -un, change to match their noun; the others never change.

sections.heading: Matching the noun
sections.body: An adjective like સારું (good) changes its ending to match the gender and number of its noun: -o for masculine, -ee for feminine, -un for neuter, and the plural endings too. The noun itself doesn't need that ending: સારી બહેન (a good sister), સારું ઘર (a good house).

examples.en: My younger sister is at home.

sections.heading: After the noun, too
sections.body: The adjective still matches when it comes after the noun, just before છે.

sections.heading: Words that never change
sections.body: All other adjectives stay the same with every noun: લાલ (red), ગરમ (hot), સુંદર (beautiful), હોશિયાર (clever). That includes ones that always end in -ee, like ગુલાબી (pink) and દુઃખી (sad): દુઃખી છોકરો, દુઃખી છોકરી.

sections.heading: Bigger, biggest
sections.body: To compare, put **કરતાં** (than) after the thing you're comparing with. For "the most", put **સૌથી** before the adjective. The adjective itself keeps its normal form.

examples.gu: આ ઘર તે ઘર કરતાં મોટું છે.
examples.tr: aa ghar te ghar kartaan moTun chhe.
examples.en: This house is bigger than that house.

examples.gu: મારો ભાઈ મારા કરતાં મોટો છે.
examples.tr: maaro bhaai maaraa kartaan moTo chhe.
examples.en: My brother is older than me.

title: Present tense
summary: How to say what you do, usually or right now, with the verb ending that matches the person.

sections.heading: I speak, she eats
sections.body:
Take the dictionary form, drop the **-vun** (બોલવું → બોલ) to get the stem, add the ending for the person, then the matching છું / છે / છો / છીએ. Stems that end in a vowel, like ખા (eat) and જા (go), slip in a y sound in some forms.

The same form means both "I eat" and "I am eating": હું ખાઉં છું can be either.

examples.en: We are going to the market.
They go for a walk every day.

sections.heading: Right now: ખાઈ રહ્યો છું
sections.body: To stress that something is happening at this very moment, use the verb's -ee form (બોલી, ખાઈ, કરી) with **રહ્યો** + છું / છે. રહ્યો matches the person doing it: રહ્યો for a man, **રહી** for a woman, **રહ્યા** for men or polite તમે.

examples.en: I'm eating right now (a man speaking).

examples.gu: બહેન ફોન પર વાત કરી રહી છે.
examples.tr: bahen phon par vaat karee rahee chhe.
examples.en: My sister is talking on the phone.

sections.heading: The -to form
sections.body: Verbs also have a form ending in **-to** (ખાતો, જતો, વાંચતો) that matches the person's gender. You need it for "don't" (હું નથી ખાતો, on the next page), for "was doing" (હું વાંચતો હતો), and with **હોઉં / હોય** for something going on at the time of something else.

examples.en: I don't eat meat (a man speaking).

examples.gu: હું રસોઈ કરતી હોઉં ત્યારે બાળકો બહાર રમે છે.
examples.tr: hun rasoi kartee houn tyaare baaLko bahaar rame chhe.
examples.en: While I'm cooking, the children play outside (a woman speaking).

title: Saying no and not
summary: Gujarati has three words for "not", and each goes with different verb forms.

sections.heading: નથી: am not, is not, are not
sections.body: **નથી** takes the place of છું, છે, છો and છીએ. It is the same for every person.

sections.heading: Don't: નથી with the -to form
sections.body: For "don't" in the present, use **નથી** with the -to form of the verb (ખાતો, ખાતી, ખાતા), and drop છું / છે / છો completely. Never say નથી છું. નથી can go before or after the verb.

examples.en: We don't speak English at home.

sections.heading: ન and નહીં
sections.body:
**ન** goes right before the verb in commands and in the past: ન જાઓ (don't go), ન આવ્યો (didn't come). In speech you'll also hear નહીં after a past verb: આવ્યો નહીં.

**નહીં** is "won't". Put it before the short form of the verb, the one in "shall I?" questions (જાઉં, આવું, કરું): હું નહીં આવું. Or put it after the future: હું આવીશ નહીં. Plain **ના** is "no".

title: Asking questions
summary: Question words go where the answer would go, and yes/no questions just rise at the end.

sections.heading: Question words
sections.body: Gujarati doesn't move the question word to the front. Put it where the answer would go, usually just before the verb: "You where are going?"

sections.heading: Which and how much match too
sections.body:
**કયું** (which) and **કેટલું** (how much) change like adjectives: **કયો** with a masculine noun, **કઈ** with a feminine one, કયું with a neuter one, and કેટલો / કેટલી / કેટલું the same way.

**કેમ** usually means "why", but in કેમ છો? it means "how".

examples.en: How much sugar should I put in the tea?

sections.heading: Yes or no
sections.body: For a yes/no question, keep the normal sentence and let your voice rise at the end. You can also start with **શું**, which here simply marks a question. Add **ને?** at the end for "right?".

title: Past tense: I went, I came
summary: Verbs like go, come and sit form the past by matching the subject's gender and number, and હતો means "was".

sections.heading: I went: matching the subject
sections.body:
For verbs with no object (go, come, sit, sleep, get up), the past form matches the subject the way an adjective does. A man says હું ગયો; a woman says હું ગઈ. A group of girls or women also takes ગઈ: છોકરીઓ ગઈ.

Most verbs make the past with **-yo**: આવવું → આવ્યો, આવી, આવ્યું, આવ્યા, આવ્યાં. A few are irregular: જવું → ગયો, બેસવું → બેઠો, સૂવું → સૂતો.
table: one woman or girl, or several
men, a man you respect, or polite તમે
a mixed group, neuter plurals, or a woman you respect

examples.en: I went to the temple yesterday (a man speaking).
She came home in the evening.
Grandma and Grandpa went to Mumbai.

sections.heading: Was and were: હતો
sections.body: **હતો** is the past of છે. It matches gender and number, not the person: હતો, હતી, હતું, હતા, હતાં. The "not" form is **નહોતો** (નહોતી, નહોતું, નહોતા).

examples.en: I was at home yesterday (a man speaking).

sections.heading: Was doing, used to do
sections.body: The -to form with હતો means "was doing" or "used to do". The rest of the sentence tells you which.

examples.en: I was watching TV (a man speaking).
We used to live in the village.
Grandma used to tell a story every day.

title: Past tense: I ate, I saw
summary: With verbs that act on something, "I" becomes મેં and the verb matches the thing, not the person.

sections.heading: મેં, તેં, તેણે
sections.body:
With verbs that act on something (eat, drink, see, do, write, say), the past works differently. The person doing it takes a special form, and a noun adds **-e** (એ): મમ્મીએ, કાગડાએ.

Verbs of movement never do this: it's always હું ગયો, never મેં ગયો. A few everyday verbs with an object skip it too, and match the person like ગયો: **લાવવું** (bring), **મળવું** (meet), **બોલવું** (speak), **ભૂલવું** (forget). So it's પપ્પા મીઠાઈ લાવ્યા and હું રવિને મળ્યો.

sections.heading: The verb matches the object
sections.body: Here the verb doesn't care who did it. It matches the thing: ચા is feminine, so ચા પીધી; પત્ર is masculine, so પત્ર લખ્યો; શાક is neuter, so શાક બનાવ્યું. A man and a woman say exactly the same sentence.

sections.heading: No object, or a person with ને
sections.body:
With no object, or when the object is a whole sentence ("he said that ..."), use the neuter -un form: મેં ખાધું (I ate). For "haven't", add નથી: મેં ખાધું નથી.

When the object is a person marked with **ને**, the verb still matches that person: ચોર (thief) is masculine, so ચોરને પકડ્યો. Polite તમને takes the plural, જોયા (to a woman, જોયાં).

examples.en: He said that he would come.

title: Future tense
summary: How to say what will happen, and how to talk about plans with જવાનો છું.

sections.heading: I will go
sections.body:
Add the future ending to the stem. In careful Gujarati, હું and તું share a form (જઈશ); in casual speech you'll also hear તું જશે.

For "will be", use હોઈશ, હશે, હોઈશું, હશો. **હશે** also means "probably, must be".

examples.en: I will go to Mumbai tomorrow.
She will call in the evening.

sections.heading: Plans: જવાનો છું
sections.body: For something already planned, use the dictionary form with **-aano** in place of -un, then છું / છે: જવાનો છું (I'm going to go). It matches the person: **જવાનો** for a man, **જવાની** for a woman, **જવાના** for men or polite તમે.

examples.gu: હું આવતા અઠવાડિયે ભારત જવાનો છું.
examples.tr: hun aavtaa aThvaaDiye bhaarat javaano chhun.
examples.en: I'm going to India next week (a man speaking).
She is going to cook today.
We are going to buy a new house.

sections.heading: Won't
sections.body: For "won't", put **નહીં** before the short form of the verb (જાઉં, આવું, કરું), or after the future form.

title: In, on, to, from
summary: Gujarati puts little words like "in" and "to" after the noun, and some nouns change shape in front of them.

sections.heading: After the noun
sections.body: Where English says "in the house", Gujarati says "house-in": ઘરમાં. These words are called postpositions because they come after. માં, ને, થી and એ join onto the word; the others, even short પર, are written as separate words.

examples.en: The key is in the pocket.
The book is on the table.

sections.heading: The oblique form
sections.body: In front of a postposition, a masculine noun ending in -o changes it to -aa, and a neuter noun ending in -un changes it to -aa too. This changed shape is called the **oblique form**: the form a word takes before a postposition. Other nouns don't change.

examples.en: The crow dropped stones into the pot.

sections.heading: Words in front change too
sections.body:
Adjectives and words like મારું go oblique along with their noun: મોટું ઘર → મોટા ઘરમાં, મારો ભાઈ → મારા ભાઈ સાથે.

Longer postpositions like **પાછળ** (behind) and **નીચે** (under) often take **ની** in between: ઘરની પાછળ.

examples.en: We live in a big house.

examples.gu: હું મારા ભાઈ સાથે રહું છું.
examples.tr: hun maaraa bhaai saathe rahun chhun.

examples.en: The cat is under the table.
The garden is behind the house.

title: My, your, his
summary: The words for my, your and 's change their ending to match the thing owned, not the owner.

sections.heading: My, your, our
sections.body: Each of these words ends like an adjective, and it matches the thing owned: મારો ભાઈ (brother, masculine), મારી બહેન (sister, feminine), મારું ઘર (house, neuter). For more than one: મારા ભાઈઓ, મારી બહેનો, મારાં ઘર.

sections.heading: 's: નો, ની, નું
sections.body: For a noun owner, add **નો / ની / નું / ના / નાં** to it, matching the thing owned: સીતાનો ભાઈ, સીતાની બહેન, સીતાનું ઘર. An owner ending in -o takes its oblique form first: છોકરો → છોકરાનું નામ.

examples.en: The capital of Gujarat is Gandhinagar.

sections.heading: Respect for elders
sections.body: Elders you respect are spoken of in the plural, so the possessive takes the plural ending: **મારા પપ્પા**, **મારા દાદા**, never મારો. For women, careful Gujarati uses **મારાં બા**, **મારાં મમ્મી**; in everyday talk you'll also hear મારી મમ્મી.

examples.en: My grandmother lives in the village.

title: Asking and telling
summary: How to tell or ask someone to do something, from friendly to very polite.

sections.heading: Three levels
sections.body: The bare stem is a friendly command for someone you call તું. Add **-o** for તમે. Add **-jo** for a gentle request, often about later; that's why goodbye is આવજો, "do come (again)". To someone you call તું, the gentle form ends in **-je**: આવજે.

sections.heading: Very polite: a question in the future
sections.body:
To ask a favour politely, use the તમે future form as a question: આપશો? (would you give?). **જરા** (a little) softens any request, and **મહેરબાની કરીને** or **કૃપા કરીને** is a formal "please".

**ચાલો** with the આપણે form means "let's".

examples.en: Could you give me some water?
Could you speak a little more slowly?

sections.heading: Don't
sections.body: Put **ન** before the command: ન આવો (don't come). A softer "please don't" is the future form + **નહીં**: ગભરાશો નહીં.

title: I like, I know, I need
summary: Many feelings in Gujarati happen "to" you: the person takes the ને form and the verb goes with the thing.

sections.heading: મને: to me
sections.body: For "I like tea", Gujarati says "to me, tea is pleasing": મને ચા ગમે છે. The person takes the ને form, and the verb goes with the thing (the tea), not with you, so it's છે, not છું.

sections.heading: Like, know how, know, need
sections.body:
**ગમવું** is to like. **આવડવું** is to know how to do something, like a skill or a language. **ખબર** is knowing a fact. **જોઈએ** is wanting or needing something.

In the past, ગમવું matches the thing you liked: મને ફિલ્મ ગમી (ફિલ્મ is feminine).

sections.heading: Hunger, cold and pain
sections.body:
**લાગવું** is for feelings that come over you. For hunger and thirst Gujarati uses the past with છે: મને ભૂખ લાગી છે, "hunger has struck me", means I'm hungry now.

મને લાગે છે કે ... means "I think that ...".

examples.gu: મને લાગે છે કે વરસાદ પડશે.
examples.tr: mane laage chhe ke varsaad paDshe.

title: Can, must, want to
summary: How to say that you can, have to, want to or should do something.

sections.heading: Can: શકવું
sections.body: Put the main verb in its -ee form (બોલી, ખાઈ, જઈ, કરી) and add **શકવું** with the normal endings. Past: શક્યો, શકી, શક્યા.
table: I won't be able to come.

examples.gu: હું થોડું ગુજરાતી બોલી શકું છું.
examples.tr: hun thoDun gujaraatee bolee shakun chhun.
examples.en: I can speak a little Gujarati.
I couldn't come yesterday (a man speaking).

sections.heading: Have to: મારે જવું પડશે
sections.body: For "have to", the person takes the **-e** form (મારે, તારે, અમારે, આપણે, તમારે), then comes the dictionary form of the verb, then **પડે** (have to), **પડશે** (will have to) or **પડ્યું** (had to).

examples.gu: મારે રોજ બસમાં જવું પડે છે.
examples.tr: maare roj basmaan javun paDe chhe.
examples.en: I have to go by bus every day.

sections.heading: Want to and should
sections.body:
**મારે** + the dictionary form + **છે** means "I want to": મારે ઘરે જવું છે. Use **જોઈએ** instead of છે for "should".

If the verb has an object, its ending matches the object: ચા is feminine, so ચા પીવી; આરામ (rest) is masculine, so આરામ કરવો. The same goes for "have to": મારે દવા લેવી પડી (I had to take medicine).

title: Helper verbs
summary: Gujarati often adds a second verb like જવું or લેવું to add a shade of meaning, such as finishing or doing something for yourself.

sections.heading: How they're built
sections.body: Take the main verb's -ee form (ખાઈ, લખી, ભૂલી) and add a helper verb that carries all the endings. The helper loses its own meaning and adds a feeling of finishing, suddenness or direction. Without it the sentence is still correct, just plainer.

sections.heading: લેવું and દેવું
sections.body: **લેવું** points the action back toward you: do it for yourself, get it done. **દેવું** points it away, toward someone else or out of your hands. Both are very common in requests: ખાઈ લો, કરી દો.

sections.heading: The helper decides મેં or હું
sections.body: In the past, the helper decides whether the subject takes the -e form. With **જવું** it doesn't: તે બધું ખાઈ ગયો. With **નાખવું**, **લેવું** or **દેવું** it does, and the verb matches the object: તેણે બધું ખાઈ નાખ્યું.

title: And, but, because, if
summary: The words that join two ideas into one sentence.

sections.heading: And, but, because, so
sections.body: **પણ** means "but" between two sentences, and "also, too" right after a word: હું પણ આવીશ (I'll come too).

examples.gu: હું ચા પીઉં છું અને તે કૉફી પીએ છે.
examples.tr: hun chaa peeun chhun ane te kophee piye chhe.
examples.en: I drink tea and he drinks coffee.

examples.gu: મને ભૂખ લાગી છે, પણ સમય નથી.
examples.tr: mane bhookh laagee chhe, paN samay nathee.
examples.en: I'm hungry, but there's no time.

examples.gu: હું આજે ઘરે છું, કારણ કે મને તાવ છે.
examples.tr: hun aaje ghare chhun, kaaraN ke mane taav chhe.
examples.en: I'm at home today because I have a fever.

examples.gu: વરસાદ પડતો હતો, એટલે અમે ઘરે રહ્યા.
examples.tr: varsaad paDto hato, eTle ame ghare rahyaa.
examples.en: It was raining, so we stayed home.

sections.heading: If … then: જો … તો
sections.body: Start the "if" part with **જો** and the result with **તો**. Gujarati often uses the future in both halves, where English uses the present after "if". **હોય** is the usual form of "is" after જો.

examples.gu: જો વરસાદ પડશે, તો અમે ઘરે રહીશું.
examples.tr: jo varsaad paDshe, to ame ghare raheeshun.
examples.en: If it rains, we'll stay home.

examples.gu: જો તમે આવશો, તો મજા આવશે.
examples.tr: jo tame aavsho, to majaa aavshe.
examples.en: If you come, it will be fun.

examples.gu: જો સમય હોય, તો ફોન કરજો.
examples.tr: jo samay hoy, to phon karjo.
examples.en: If you have time, give me a call.

sections.heading: When … then: જ્યારે … ત્યારે
sections.body: **જ્યારે** (when) opens the first part and **ત્યારે** (then) opens the second. After verbs like say, think and know, **કે** means "that".

examples.gu: જ્યારે હું નાનો હતો, ત્યારે અમે ગામમાં રહેતા હતા.
examples.tr: jyaare hun naano hato, tyaare ame gaammaan rahetaa hataa.
examples.en: When I was little, we lived in the village (a man speaking).

examples.gu: જ્યારે પપ્પા આવશે, ત્યારે આપણે જમીશું.
examples.tr: jyaare pappaa aavshe, tyaare aapNe jameeshun.

examples.gu: મને ખબર છે કે તમે વ્યસ્ત છો.
examples.tr: mane khabar chhe ke tame vyast chho.
examples.en: I know that you are busy.

title: Numbers, time and dates
summary: Telling the time, the special words for quarters and halves, and saying the day and the date.

sections.heading: What time is it?
sections.body: Ask **કેટલા વાગ્યા?** (literally "how many have struck?"). Answer with the number and **વાગ્યા છે**; one o'clock is singular, **એક વાગ્યો છે**. For "at" a time, use **વાગ્યે**.

examples.en: I get up at seven o'clock.

sections.heading: Quarter past, half past, quarter to
sections.body:
**સવા** adds a quarter, **સાડા** adds a half, and **પોણા** takes a quarter away. Half past one and half past two have their own words: **દોઢ** and **અઢી**.

The same words work for money and amounts: દોઢસો is 150, અઢીસો is 250, and સાડા ત્રણસો is 350.

examples.en: The train will come at quarter to eight.
We'll eat at half past one.

examples.gu: આ સાડી અઢી હજાર રૂપિયાની છે.
examples.tr: aa saaDee aDhee hajaar roopiyaanee chhe.
examples.en: This sari costs two thousand five hundred rupees.

sections.heading: Days and dates
sections.body: The days of the week all end in **વાર**. For the date, say the number and **તારીખ**. Remember that **કાલે** means both yesterday and tomorrow; the verb tells you which.
